segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: At that very time some people were there who told him about the Galileans whose blood Pilate had mixed with their sacrifices.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He answered them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Do you think that these Galileans were worse sinners than all the other Galileans because they suffered these things?

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: No, I tell you; but unless you turn back, you will all perish in a similar way.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Or those eighteen on whom the tower in Siloam fell and killed them: do you think that they were worse debtors than all the other people living in Jerusalem?

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: No, I tell you; but unless you turn back, you will all perish in the same way.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then he told this parable:

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “A man had a fig tree planted in his vineyard, and he came looking for fruit on it and found none.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: So he said to the vinedresser, ‘Look, for three years now I have been coming to look for fruit on this fig tree and I find none. Cut it down! Why should it use up the ground as well?’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But he answered him, ‘Sir, leave it this year too, until I dig around it and put on manure.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And if it bears fruit in the coming year, good; but if not, you can cut it down.’”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He was teaching in one of the synagogues on the Sabbath.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And there was a woman who had had a spirit of infirmity for eighteen years; she was bent over and completely unable to straighten up.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When Jesus saw her, he called her over and said to her,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Woman, you are released from your infirmity,”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and he laid his hands on her. At once she was straightened up, and she began to glorify God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But the synagogue leader, indignant that Jesus had healed on the Sabbath, spoke up and said to the crowd,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “There are six days on which work ought to be done. So come and be healed on those days, and not on the Sabbath day.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But the Lord answered him and said,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Hypocrites! Does not each of you on the Sabbath untie his ox or his donkey from the manger and lead it off to give it water?

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And this woman, a daughter of Abraham, whom Satan bound—look, for eighteen years—ought she not to have been untied from this bond on the Sabbath day?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: As he said these things, all his opponents were put to shame, and the whole crowd rejoiced at all the glorious things being done by him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So he said,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “What is the kingdom of God like, and to what shall I compare it?

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: It is like a mustard seed that a man took and put in his own garden; and it grew and became a tree, and the birds of the sky nested in its branches.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And again he said,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “To what shall I compare the kingdom of God?

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: It is like leaven that a woman took and hid in three measures of flour until all of it was leavened.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He went on through one town and village after another, teaching and making his way to Jerusalem.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Someone said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Lord, are those who are being saved few?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Strive to enter through the narrow door, because many, I tell you, will seek to enter and will not be able,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: once the master of the house has risen and shut the door, and you begin to stand outside and knock on the door, saying, ‘Lord, open to us!’ Then he will answer you, ‘I do not know you or where you are from.’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Then you will begin to say, ‘We ate and drank in your presence, and you taught in our streets.’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And he will say to you, ‘I do not know where you are from. Get away from me, all you workers of wrongdoing!’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: There will be weeping and gnashing of teeth there, when you see Abraham and Isaac and Jacob and all the prophets in the kingdom of God, but yourselves being cast out.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And people will come from east and west and from north and south and will recline at table in the kingdom of God.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And look, there are some who are last who will be first, and some who are first who will be last.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: At that very hour some Pharisees came up and said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Get out and go on your way from here, because Herod wants to kill you.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Go and tell that fox, ‘Look, I am casting out demons and completing healings today and tomorrow, and on the third day I am brought to completion.’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Nevertheless, I must go on my way today and tomorrow and the day after, because it cannot be that a prophet should perish outside Jerusalem.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Jerusalem, Jerusalem, the city that kills the prophets and stones those sent to her! How often I wanted to gather your children the way a hen gathers her own brood under her wings, and you did not want it.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Look, your house is left to you. And I tell you, you will certainly not see me until the time comes when you say, ‘Blessed is the one who comes in the name of the Lord.’”

notes.phrase: whose blood Pilate had mixed with their sacrifices
notes.note: The phrase means that Pilate, the Roman governor of Judea, had Galilean pilgrims killed while they were offering sacrifices, presumably at the temple in Jerusalem. No other surviving source records this incident, nor the collapse of the tower in verse 4. Both are raised here against the common assumption that sudden disaster shows its victims to have been especially sinful.

Most translations keep “repent” as an established term that includes a change of life. In current English, though, “repent” centres on feeling sorry, whereas the Greek word in the Gospels carries the prophets' call to return to God: a change of direction in mind and conduct. “Turn back” is used for that reason.

The Greek word means someone who owes a debt. Jewish speech of the period commonly spoke of sin as a debt owed to God, and the word here stands in parallel with “sinners” in verse 2; most translations therefore paraphrase it as “offenders” or “guilty”. The debt image is kept because it is what the Greek says, and it follows directly on the sayings about the debtor's prison at the end of the previous chapter.

notes.traditional: could in no wise lift up herself / could not fully straighten herself
notes.note: The closing Greek phrase (“to the full”) can go with “unable”, meaning she could not straighten up at all, or with “straighten up”, meaning she could not straighten up fully. Translations are divided, and the Greek does not settle it.

Jesus' argument turns on repeated words. The same Greek verb is used for untying the ox in verse 15 and for freeing the woman here, and “bound” and “bond” share a root in Greek as in English. “Ought” likewise picks up the synagogue leader's own word in verse 14: he says work ought to be done on six days, and Jesus replies that this release ought to have happened on the Sabbath.

notes.phrase: the birds of the sky nested in its branches
notes.traditional: the fowls of the air lodged in the branches of it
notes.note: The wording echoes Old Testament pictures of a great kingdom as a tree in whose branches the birds find shelter (Ezekiel 17:23; 31:6; Daniel 4:12, 21). A hearer who knew those passages would catch the suggestion of a realm that grows from a tiny seed to give shelter to the nations.

The measure named is the saton, a dry measure commonly estimated at about thirteen litres. Three of them make a very large batch of dough, enough bread for well over a hundred people. The scale is part of the point of the comparison.

notes.phrase: once the master of the house has risen and shut the door
notes.traditional: When once the master of the house is risen up, and hath shut to the door
notes.note: Ancient manuscripts had no punctuation, and it is unclear whether this clause finishes the sentence of verse 24 (many will be unable to enter once the door is shut) or begins a new one (“Once the master has shut the door, you will begin to stand outside…”). The translation follows the punctuation of the SBL edition, which joins it to verse 24. Many English versions begin a new sentence here.

Herod here is Herod Antipas, ruler of Galilee and Perea under Rome, who had executed John the Baptist. In Greek usage the fox was a byword for cunning. In Jewish usage it could also stand for a destructive or an insignificant creature, as against a lion. Which nuance is uppermost here is debated; the epithet is contemptuous either way.

notes.traditional: I shall be perfected / I finish my course
notes.note: The Greek verb can be read as passive (“I am brought to completion”, with God as the implied agent) or as middle (“I finish”, “I reach my goal”). It shares a root with “completing” earlier in the verse, which the translation keeps. Most interpreters see an allusion to Jesus' death in Jerusalem as the goal of his work, and “today, tomorrow and the third day” is generally taken as an idiom for a short, fixed time.

notes.phrase: your house is left to you
notes.traditional: your house is left unto you desolate
notes.note: Many later manuscripts add “desolate”, probably under the influence of Matthew 23:38 and Jeremiah 22:5; the earliest witnesses to Luke lack it, and the SBL text omits it. The sense is that the house is abandoned to its occupants' own keeping. “House” may mean the temple, the city, or the nation; interpreters differ. The closing words quote Psalm 118:26.

candidates.reason: The vocative ranges from polite “Sir” to “Lord” as a title, and in parables the two shade into each other, so a rule is needed for when each is used.
It recurs across the New Testament as perish, be destroyed, be lost or die, and readers draw theological conclusions from which English word appears.
Translations vary among unrighteousness, injustice, iniquity, evil and wrongdoing, and the choice should be aligned with the rendering of the δίκαιος word group.
Traditionally “perfect”, which misleads modern readers; it is important in Luke, John and above all Hebrews and needs one consistent rendering.
It covers both illness and weakness across the Gospels and Paul, where the English choice (weakness, sickness, infirmity, disability) affects how passages are read.
